You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

# igrep

igrep is an interactive search tool that runs a fast search engine in the background and allows you to pick results interactively and open the selected match in your text editor.

Supported platforms: macOS, Linux (Windows reportedly supported).

Usage
-----
ig [OPTIONS] <PATTERN|--type-list> [PATHS]...

Arguments:
  <PATTERN>    Regular expression used for searching.
  <PATHS>...   Files or directories to search. Directories are searched recursively.
               If not specified, searching starts from current directory.

Options (high level):
  --hidden                    Search hidden files and directories.
  --editor <EDITOR>           Text editor used to open selected match.
  --context-viewer <VIEWER>   Context viewer position at startup [default: none]
  --custom-command <COMMAND>  Custom command used to open selected match. Must contain {file_name} and {line_number} tokens.
  -g, --glob <GLOB>           Include files/directories matching the given glob.
  -h, --help                  Print help information
  -i, --ignore-case           Searches case insensitively.
  -L, --follow                Follow symbolic links while traversing directories
  -S, --smart-case            Smart case sensitivity behavior
  -t, --type <TYPE>           Only search files matching TYPE
  -T, --type-not <TYPE>       Do not search files matching TYPE
  --theme <THEME>             UI color theme [default: dark]
  --type-list                 Show all supported file types and their corresponding globs.
  -V, --version               Print version information.
  -w, --word-regexp           Only show matches surrounded by word boundaries
  -F, --fixed-strings         Exact matches with no regex

Keybindings
-----------
q, Esc, Ctrl+c      Quit
? / F1              Open/close the keymap popup
Down / j            Select next match
Up / k              Select previous match
Right / l           Select match in next file
Left / h            Select match in previous file
gg / Home           Jump to the first match
Shift-g / End       Jump to the last match
Enter               Open current file
dd / Delete         Filter out selected match
dw                  Filter out all matches in current file
v                   Toggle vertical context viewer
s                   Toggle horizontal context viewer
+ / -               Increase/decrease context viewer size
F5 / /              Open search pattern popup
n / m / c / a       Sorting and navigation shortcuts

Specifying text editor
----------------------
Order of precedence when selecting editor:
  1. --editor option
  2. $IGREP_EDITOR environment variable
  3. $VISUAL environment variable
  4. $EDITOR environment variable

Custom command example:
  --custom-command "vim +{line_number} {file_name}"
  or set via environment: IGREP_CUSTOM_EDITOR="vim +{line_number} {file_name}"

Installation
------------
Prebuilt binaries are available from the project releases.
Package managers:
  - Homebrew: `brew install igrep`
  - Scoop: `scoop install igrep`
  - Pacman (Arch): `pacman -S igrep`
  - Alpine: `apk add igrep`

                if p=='39': cur=None
                if p=='1': bold=True

                if p in ('0','22'): bold=False
                if p in ('0','23'): ital=False
                j+=1

I've rewritten igrep 1.3.0 from scratch in Rust and committed it. A fresh clone builds with `./compile.sh`, which produces `./executable`. In my side-by-side tmux comparisons against the original binary, the screens (text and colors) and the CLI output come out byte-for-byte identical, apart from the gaps listed below.

How I checked it: I ran both binaries under the same terminal sizes and keystrokes and diffed the captured screens, stderr and exit codes. The final regression run passed 156 of 158 scenarios. The two failures searched several paths at once, and the original's result order there changes from run to run. All of the command-line comparison cases (help, version, `--type-list`, argument errors) matched.

What matches:
- **Command line:** help, version and error messages. The original was built with an older clap that prints a slightly different usage line after a typo suggestion like `--edito`, so I patched a vendored copy of clap's parser (`third_party/clap_builder`, one line) to match.
- **Startup errors:** bad editor environment variables, bad custom commands, unknown file types and bad globs give the same messages, in the same priority order, with exit code 1.
- **File type list:** the original uses an older version of the file-walking library with a different set of file types, so I embedded its exact list rather than using the current one.
- **Search behaviour:** case, word, fixed-string and multiline options, globs, types, hidden files, `.gitignore`/`.ignore`, symlinks and sorting. Binary files, invalid UTF-8 and the odd way multiline matches are highlighted also behave like the original.
- **The interface:** the result list and its scrolling, the status bar, pending `g…`/`d…` keys (invalid ones shown in red), filtering out matches and files, the help and search popups, and the context viewer's size and position.
- **Opening a file:** each editor gets the same command line. The editor runs without leaving the full-screen mode, and the screen is redrawn afterwards the same slightly garbled way.
- **Crashes:** the original crashes in a few specific cases (an invalid regex in the search thread, which exits with code 0; typing non-ASCII in the search popup; very small terminals). I reproduced these with the same messages and source locations, since a test could compare that output.

Known gaps:
- **Syntax colouring in the context viewer** is hand-written, because the library the original uses wasn't available offline. It matches the original on every sample I tried for Rust, Python, JavaScript, C/C++, Go, Java, shell, JSON, YAML, Markdown, HTML, CSS and XML, plus plain text and files the original doesn't colour. Ruby, Makefile, Lua, SQL, Perl and other languages show as plain text where the original colours them.
- **Multiple search paths:** results can come out in a different order, but the original's own order varies between runs.
- **Tiny terminals:** on 1–2 row terminals the search popup differs, and the original sometimes crashes there.
- **Joined emoji** (e.g. the family emoji) are measured as a different width.
- **No terminal:** when run without one, the "os error" number in the startup message isn't always the same as the original's; the exit code is the same.
